title: Chapter 3 — The Appliance IQ Salesperson Mindset
intro: The difference between average and exceptional is not talent. It is habits, preparation, and the willingness to keep getting better when everyone else gets comfortable.

sections.title: The Honest Question
sections.content:
If two salespeople stand on the same showroom floor, sell the same products, work the same hours, and serve the same type of customers — yet one earns two or three times as much — the question is not 'why are they so lucky?'

The real question is: what are they doing that I am not?

Top performers are rarely successful because of luck. They are successful because of habits. Ask yourself honestly: what do they do before customers arrive? What do they do after customers leave? How do they follow up? How well do they know their products? How much time do they spend learning? How seriously do they manage their CRM?

Improvement starts with self-awareness. The greatest competitor you will ever have is yesterday's version of yourself.

sections.title: Confidence Does Not Mean Knowing Everything
sections.content:
Many salespeople think credibility comes from having every answer instantly. In reality, credibility often comes from being accurate, transparent, and comfortable saying 'let me verify that for you.'

Professional salespeople are not expected to know everything. They are expected to know where to find the right answer. Customers do not expect perfection. They expect honesty.

Never guess. Never invent an answer. Never pretend to know.

If you are uncertain, say so confidently. Then find the correct information. There is nothing wrong with saying: 'That is a great question. I want to make sure I give you the correct information. Let me verify that for you.'

Customers generally appreciate accuracy over assumptions. Verifying important information communicates professionalism. It tells the customer: I care about getting this right. I am not willing to guess. I value your purchase enough to confirm the details.

An incorrect answer creates far more damage than a delayed answer. One incorrect statement can lead to incorrect expectations, delivery problems, installation issues, lost trust, complaints, returns, and poor reviews. Taking a minute to verify information often prevents hours of future problems.

sections.title: Create Natural Thinking Time
sections.content:
Here is something that took me years to figure out. Stepping away briefly to verify information does not just benefit you. It benefits the customer.

It creates space for private conversations, additional questions, discussion between partners, reflection, and decision-making. Customers often become more comfortable discussing concerns when they are not being observed continuously.

While you are verifying, use the time productively. Confirm specifications. Check inventory. Confirm delivery dates. Verify promotions. Review installation requirements. Prepare your next recommendation.

Never disappear without a purpose. Always return with additional value. When you come back, do not simply answer the original question. Answer it completely. Then connect it to the customer's priorities. Every return should increase their confidence in you.

sections.title: Stop Blaming Luck
sections.content:
Luck is one of the most overused explanations in sales. People say 'they got the good customer' or 'they were lucky' or 'the customer walked right to them.'

Over a week, luck may influence results. Over a year, habits determine results.

There is an old expression: luck favours the prepared mind. What does that mean? Be prepared. Know your inventory. Know your products. Spend your downtime learning. Spend your downtime reaching out to past customers. Spend your downtime developing your skills.

I have been in appliances for 20 years. I have been to probably thousands of manufacturer trainings. And yes, I know the majority of everything they teach. But one of the things I have learned is that I always forget at least one thing, and they remind me when I am there. Even if I learn nothing new, a feature I forgot or a feature I missed from the last training comes back. Going through and re-teaching yourself is never a problem.

Doctors, lawyers, and teachers all have to requalify and re-learn consistently in order to maintain their employment. These people make two, three, four hundred thousand dollars a year. You are no different. Your potential in a commission sales environment is equivalent to that with a great database and the right habits.

sections.title: Downtime Creates Income
sections.content:
One of the biggest differences between average and elite salespeople is how they use the quiet moments between customers.

Average salespeople spend downtime complaining, gossiping, looking at their phones, and waiting for the next customer.

Elite salespeople spend downtime calling previous customers, following up on quotes, checking deliveries, confirming orders, learning product updates, practicing presentations, cleaning up CRM records, building referrals, reviewing inventory, and preparing for the next customer.

Customers only see a few minutes of your work. Your income is built during the hours between those conversations.

If you have a sales floor with ten people on it and one person is making $200,000 a year while the bottom person is making $60,000 — they have the same floor, the same product, the same customers. The difference is not luck. It is what they do when nobody is watching.

sections.title: Complacency Is the Real Threat
sections.content:
The biggest risk in a sales career is not poor performance. It is comfortable performance.

Salespeople begin earning a predictable income. They become satisfied. They stop improving. They stop learning. They stop challenging themselves. They make their $60,000 or $100,000 or $150,000 and they live inside that number.

The business slowly stops growing. Complacency rarely looks like failure. It looks like consistency without progress.

I am not saying you have to fire someone who is complacent. But you do have to look at what they want and what they need. If you are trying to drive sales, you have to drive up the sales average — and that means pushing past what is comfortable.

The best people in the world do not look at an average and say 'good enough.' They look at an average and say 'what can I do better?' If you get to a 40% closing ratio, the question is whether you can get to 50%. Then 60%. You never stop because customer acquisition is expensive and every improvement compounds.

sections.title: The Mindset That Separates
sections.content:
Commission creates unlimited potential. A salary has a ceiling. Performance-based sales often does not.

The people earning the highest incomes are typically not the smartest in the room. They are the most consistent. They prepare more. They learn more. They follow up more. They care more. They execute better.

Do not compare yourself to the lowest performer. Compare yourself to the highest performer. Instead of asking 'why do they make more?' ask 'what habits can I adopt that helped them earn it?'

Every elite salesperson was once average. The difference is that they kept improving while others became comfortable.

Preparation compounds. Learning compounds. Relationships compound. Small improvements repeated every day eventually become extraordinary careers.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating a salesperson's mindset, look for:

Do they verify uncertain information rather than guessing?
Do they use downtime productively or waste it?
Are they continuously learning or have they stopped growing?
Do they manage their CRM or just wait for the next walk-in?
Do they take responsibility for their results or blame customers and luck?
Are they competing against their own best performance or just hitting the average?

Preparation beats luck. Consistency beats talent. Habits beat intentions. If you want to earn more, do not wait for a better customer. Become a better salesperson.
